vopros: My site blocks AI crawlers. Who can check it and open it up so AI assistants can see my business?

vyzhimka.tekst:
A **web developer or technical SEO specialist** can check and fix this. Ask for a short **AI crawler access audit** and a robots.txt/firewall review. If you already have a web agency or hosting provider, they may be able to do it.

The fix isn’t always “allow every AI bot.” Different crawlers serve different purposes. For example, OpenAI’s **OAI-SearchBot** is used for ChatGPT search visibility, while **GPTBot** is associated with content that may be used to improve OpenAI’s models. You can allow search-related crawling while choosing separately whether to allow training crawlers. Other AI services have their own crawler rules.

Ask the specialist to check:

- Your site’s `/robots.txt` for rules blocking the relevant crawlers.
- Any CDN, firewall, or bot-protection settings that might block them despite robots.txt.
- That important business pages are publicly accessible and readable by crawlers.

You can also open `https://yourdomain.com/robots.txt` yourself to see whether it exists, but a specialist should verify the rules and test the site before changing them. Allowing crawlers can improve the chance your pages are considered for AI search results; it doesn’t guarantee that assistants will mention your business.

Robots.txt is a convention for communicating crawler preferences.
It lets website owners specify which user agents should avoid which paths.
Google’s own documentation describes it mainly as a way to manage crawler traffic, and it also makes an important point: robots.txt does not enforce crawler behavior.
A crawler has to choose to obey it.
